Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is a safe and effective procedure for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm, offering successful outcomes in terms of intraoperative and postoperative morbidity, hospital stay, and cosmesis for patients. This technique replicates the effectiveness of open surgical oncological principles, demonstrating similar outcomes such as survival rates and recurrence rates when treating adrenal cortical carcinoma.

However, it's essential to note that local infiltration of periadrenal tissue is a main contraindication for this approach. Experienced surgeons can perform laparoscopic adrenalectomy regardless of the size or location of the myomas.

For patients who are carefully selected, day case laparoscopic cholecystectomy provides good patient satisfaction. This procedure is safe and feasible when radiologically and intraoperatively confirmed as safe.

Residual fundus or neofundus after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy can be safely addressed with fundectomy as a revision surgery. Good results in terms of GERD symptoms control and additional weight loss have been achieved, but high rates of postoperative complications remain a concern.

Laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery is feasible, especially when hiatal herniation or breakdown of the fundoplication are suspected. Results were successful despite technical difficulties.

Robotically assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy induces lower tissue trauma than traditional retropubic radical prostatectomy.

Performing rectal anastomosis in gynaecological debulking surgery without a diverting stoma is safe, but experienced surgeons should be cautious and consider alternative options due to the risk of postoperative complications.

Laparoscopic sonography is a reliable and sensitive procedure for staging colorectal cancer, providing valuable diagnostic information. However, its accuracy may not be comparable to laparoscopy, especially in cases with tumors larger than 7 cm.

Regarding intensive chemotherapy safety for rural cancer patients, it appears safe at standard doses when administered by experienced general practitioners through phone or videoconferencing support. This approach can reduce concerns related to safety and morbidity.
